summary: Gives an overview of the Portable Document Format and updates the registration of application/pdf. It obsoletes RFC 3778.

plainLanguage.summary: PDF is the format most people mean when they say a document file. This RFC is the Internet's record of that format: which media type name to use, what a PDF file looks like at the start, how a link can point at a particular page or attachment inside a PDF, and which restricted variants exist for archiving, printing and accessibility. It replaces an earlier record from 2004.

questions: what is the application/pdf media type
subtitle: The registration of application/pdf, the file type used to exchange finished documents on the Internet.

tldr.problem: The registration of the application/pdf media type dates from 2004 and described a format then owned by one company. It needed to be brought up to date with the ISO standard, the newer PDF versions and what is now known about the security of PDF readers.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC updates the registration itself and records the facts a receiving program needs: the file name extension, the magic number at the start of a PDF, the fragment identifiers a link may carry and the subset standards a PDF may claim to follow.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational document that obsoletes RFC 3778. The change controller moved from Adobe to ISO, and the security section was rewritten to match the current understanding of PDF vulnerabilities.

facts.label: Media type
facts.value: application/pdf, with no parameters of any kind

facts.label: Magic number
facts.value: All PDF files start with %PDF- followed by the version number, such as %PDF-1.7

facts.label: Fragment identifier coordinates
facts.value: 1/72 of an inch, measured down and to the right from the upper left corner of the current page

today: RFC 8118 was published in March 2017 as an Informational document and obsoletes RFC 3778. It has not been obsoleted or updated since. The change controller for the media type moved from Adobe to ISO, and the most recent published specification named in the registration is ISO 32000-2, which is PDF 2.0.

sections.title: What application/pdf Is
sections.content:
The document provides updated information on the registration of the media type application/pdf for documents in the PDF syntax, and it obsoletes RFC 3778.

PDF was originally envisioned as a way to reliably communicate and view printed information electronically across a wide variety of machine configurations, operating systems and communication networks. It is used to represent final form formatted documents. PDF pages may include text, images, graphics and multimedia content such as video and audio. PDF is also capable of containing auxiliary structures, including annotations, bookmarks, file attachments, hyperlinks, logical structures and metadata, which are useful for navigation and for building collections of related documents, as well as for reviewing and commenting on documents. A rich JavaScript model has been defined for interacting with PDF documents.

The imaging model for PDF was originally based on the PostScript page description language, used to render complex text, images and graphics in a device-independent and resolution-independent manner. PDF supports encryption and digital signatures, and the encryption capability is combined with access control information to facilitate management of the functionality available to the recipient. It supports the inclusion of document and object-level metadata through the Extensible Metadata Platform.

The registration itself lists the type name as application and the subtype name as pdf, with no required parameters and no optional parameters, binary encoding, intended usage COMMON and no restrictions on usage. The file extension is .pdf, the Macintosh file type code is PDF, and all PDF files start with the characters %PDF- followed by the PDF version number, such as %PDF-1.7 or %PDF-2.0, in US-ASCII encoding.
sections.plainLanguage: PDF is meant for a document that is finished: it holds the text, images and layout exactly as they should appear when printed or shown. It can also carry annotations, bookmarks, attachments and links, and it can be encrypted or signed. The registration tells programs what to call the file type and what to look for at the start of the file to recognise it.

sections.title: How PDF Became an ISO Standard
sections.content:
PDF is used widely in the Internet community. The first version, PDF 1.0, was published in 1993 by Adobe Systems Incorporated. Since then PDF has grown to be a widely used format for capturing and exchanging formatted documents electronically across the Web, by email and virtually every other document-exchange mechanism.

In 2008, PDF 1.7 was adopted as an ISO standard, ISO 32000-1:2008, using the ISO Fast-Track process. That specification is technically identical to Adobe Portable Document Format version 1.7. The ISO TC-171 committee later developed a refresh of PDF known as ISO 32000-2, which is the version PDF 2.0.
sections.plainLanguage: PDF started as one company's format. In 2008 the same specification was adopted as an ISO standard, and the maintainer of the registration changed with it, so the record of the format now belongs to ISO rather than to Adobe.

sections.title: Fragment Identifiers in a PDF Link
sections.content:
Fragment identifiers appear at the end of a URI and provide a way to reference an anchor to subordinate content within the target of the URI, or additional parameters to the process of opening the identified content. A PDF fragment identifier has one or more parameters, separated by the ampersand or pound character. Each parameter consists of the parameter name, an equal sign, and the parameter value; lists of values are comma-separated, and parameter value strings may be URI-encoded. Parameters are processed left to right. The specification of fragment identifiers for PDF appeared originally in RFC 3778 and is now included in ISO 32000-2, and the RFC's section is a summary of that material, with any disagreement resolved in favour of the ISO definition.

Coordinate values are expressed in the default user space coordinate system of the document: 1/72 of an inch measured down and to the right from the upper left corner of the current page.

Several parameters identify subordinate content of a PDF file and may also set the document view to make the identified content visible. The page parameter identifies a physical page, where the first page has a value of 1. The nameddest parameter identifies a named destination. The structelem parameter identifies the structure element with the given ID key within a StructElem dictionary. The comment parameter carries the value of an annotation name, defined by the NM key in the corresponding annotation dictionary of the selected page. The ef parameter identifies the embedded file whose parameter string matches a file specification dictionary in the EmbeddedFiles name tree; if the ef parameter is not at the end of the fragment identifier, the rest of the identifier is applied to the embedded file according to its own media type, which allows identification of content within the embedded file, which itself might be a PDF file. The RFC notes that when attempting to open a PDF file that is not from a trusted source, the processor may choose to prompt the user or even prevent the file from being opened.

Other parameters operate on the view of the document when it is opened. The zoom parameter takes a scale percentage, where 100 corresponds to a zoom of 100 percent, plus optional left and top values, which must both be given if either is. The view parameter takes a keyword and position matching the PDF destination syntax. The viewrect parameter sets the view rectangle, and the highlight parameter highlights a rectangle. The search parameter opens the document and searches for one or more words, selecting the first match, with the word list quoted and individual words separated by a space or %20. The fdf parameter imports data into PDF form fields from a Forms Data Format or XML FDF file, and should be specified as the last parameter of a URI.
sections.plainLanguage: A link to a PDF can carry instructions after the pound sign: open at page four, zoom to 150 percent, highlight this rectangle, or search for a word. The instructions are read from left to right, and distances are measured in points, which are seventy-two to the inch.

sections.title: The Subset Standards
sections.content:
Several subsets of PDF have been published as distinct ISO standards. PDF/X, initially released in 2001 as PDF/X-1a, specifies how to use PDF for graphics exchange, with the aim of facilitating correct and predictable printing by print service providers. It has gone through multiple revisions, and the most recently released is part 8, specifying different levels of conformance: PDF/X-1a:2001, PDF/X-3:2002, PDF/X-1a:2003, PDF/X-3:2003, PDF/X-4, PDF/X-4p, PDF/X-5g, PDF/X-5pg and PDF/X-5n.

PDF/A, initially released in 2005, specifies how to use PDF for long-term preservation of electronic documents. It prohibits PDF features that are not well suited to long-term archiving, including JavaScript or executable file launches, and its requirements for viewers include colour management guidelines and support for embedded fonts. There are three parts and a total of eight conformance levels: PDF/A-1a, PDF/A-1b, PDF/A-2a, PDF/A-2b, PDF/A-2u, PDF/A-3a, PDF/A-3b and PDF/A-3u.

PDF/E, initially released in 2008 as PDF/E-1, specifies how to use PDF in engineering workflows such as manufacturing, construction and geospatial analysis. PDF/VT, initially released in 2010, specifies how to use PDF in variable and transactional printing; it is based on PDF/X and places additional restrictions on PDF content elements and supporting metadata, and it specifies three conformance levels, PDF/VT-1, PDF/VT-2 and PDF/VT-2s. PDF/UA, initially released in 2012 as PDF/UA-1, specifies how to create accessible electronic documents; it requires the use of the Tagged PDF feature of ISO 32000 and adds many requirements regarding semantic correctness in applying logical structures to content.

All of these subset standards use the application/pdf media type, and they are generally not exclusive, so it is possible to construct a PDF file that conforms to both PDF/A-2b and PDF/X-4. Documents claiming conformance to one or more of the subset standards use XMP metadata to identify their levels of conformance, and PDF processors should examine document metadata streams for such identifiers and, if appropriate, label documents as such when presenting them to the user.
sections.plainLanguage: Several restricted versions of PDF have become standards of their own, each aimed at a particular job: one for sending files to a print shop, one for keeping documents for decades, one for engineering drawings, one for variable printing such as invoices, and one for screen readers. All of them are still ordinary PDF files, and a file can follow more than one of these rules at once.

sections.title: Versions and How People Meet PDFs
sections.content:
The PDF format has gone through several revisions, primarily for the addition of features. PDF features have generally been added in a way that older viewers fail gracefully, because they can just ignore features they do not recognise. Even so, the older the PDF version produced, the more legacy viewers will support that version, but the fewer features will be enabled. The application/pdf media type is used for all versions.

PDF files are experienced through a reader or viewer of PDF files. For most of the common platforms in use, iOS, OS X, Windows, Android, ChromeOS and Kindle, and for most browsers, including Edge, Safari, Chrome and Firefox, PDF viewing is built in. In addition, there are many PDF viewers available for download and installation. The PDF specification was published and freely available since the format was introduced in 1993, so hundreds of companies and organizations make tools for PDF creation, viewing and manipulation.
sections.plainLanguage: Each new PDF version adds features but leaves the old ones working, so an older viewer simply ignores what it does not recognise. The media type name never changes, whatever the version inside the file. Today the ability to view a PDF is built into most operating systems and web browsers, and the format has been open and freely available since 1993.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
PDF is certainly a complex media type, which sets requirements for security analysis of media type registrations. RFC 3778, which this document obsoletes, contained a detailed analysis of some of the security issues for PDF implementations known at the time. The RFC says that while that analysis is not necessarily wrong, the threat analysis is much too limited and the mitigations are somewhat out of date, and that there is now extensive literature on security threats involving PDF implementations and how to avoid them.

The file format allows several constructs that may compromise security if handled inadequately by PDF processors. PDF may contain scripts to customise the displaying and processing of PDF files; these scripts are expressed in a version of JavaScript and are intended for execution by the PDF processor. A PDF file may refer to other PDF files for portions of content, and processors may be expected to find and use those external files. PDF may act as a container for various files embedded in it, for example as attached files, and processors may offer functionality to open and display such files or store them on the system, as with the ef open action; the PDF specification places no restrictions on the types of files that may be embedded, so processors should be extremely careful to prevent unwanted execution of attached executables or decompression of attached archives that may store dangerous files in the host file system. PDF files may contain links to content on the Internet. And the fragment identifier syntax contains directives for opening, with ef, or including, with fdf, additional material.

PDF interpreters executing any scripts or programs related to these constructs must be extremely careful to ensure that untrusted software is executed in a protected environment. The PDF processor itself, as well as its plugins and scripts, may be a source of insecurity, by either obvious or subtle means.
sections.plainLanguage: A PDF file can carry a program that runs when it is opened, it can pull in other files, and it can carry attachments of any kind at all. So the reader has to run any script it finds in a sandbox, and it has to be careful about opening what is attached. The RFC replaces an older, thinner threat analysis with a list of the constructs that have actually caused trouble.

items.label: page=pageNum
items.desc: Identifies a physical page. The first page in the document has a pageNum value of 1.

items.label: nameddest=name
items.desc: Identifies a named destination in the document.

items.label: structelem=structID
items.desc: Identifies the structure element with that ID key within a StructElem dictionary.

items.label: comment=commentID
items.desc: The value of an annotation name, defined by the NM key in the annotation dictionary of the selected page.

items.label: ef=name
items.desc: Identifies the embedded file whose name matches a file specification in the EmbeddedFiles name tree.

items.label: zoom=scale,left,top
items.desc: The percentage to zoom to, where 100 is a zoom of 100 percent, with optional left and top values.

items.label: view=keyword,position
items.desc: Arguments taken from the PDF destination syntax.

items.label: search=wordList
items.desc: Opens the document and searches for one or more words, selecting the first match.

items.label: fdf=URI
items.desc: Imports data into PDF form fields from a Forms Data Format or XML FDF file.
